summary.text: 你 is the usual written form of the singular second-person pronoun “you.” Its visible parts are 亻 on the left and 尔 on the right; one proposed analysis assigns person meaning to 亻 and a sound cue to 尔, though the evidence does not directly establish that historical construction.

formation.text: A phono-semantic analysis is plausible: 亻 contributes the person category and 尔 is proposed as the phonetic element. Another account treats 人 and 尔 as an ideographic combination meaning “person” and “you.” The inspected evidence does not resolve these proposals or directly document the construction, so the phono-semantic account remains a source interpretation rather than a demonstrated ancient analysis.

components.text: The left-side 亻 represents a person and is assigned the semantic role in the proposed phono-semantic analysis. It is the positional form of 人; no separate historical change to this form is established here.
The right-side 尔 is proposed as the phonetic element. In its own reported history, 尔 is a shortened form of 爾; this does not by itself establish its sound role in 你.

sound_limitation.text: Mandarin 尔 ěr and 你 nǐ provide a real modern reading pair, but current readings alone do not establish the historical phonetic role. The inspected Baxter–Sagart table gives 尔 as Middle Chinese nyeX and Old Chinese *n[ə][r]ʔ, but supplies no matched 你 entry in that system.

sound.text: The modern Mandarin readings ěr and nǐ are a comparison only; their similarity does not demonstrate the proposed historical relationship.

history.text: The cited character dictionaries report that 你 is absent from oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions and from Shuowen. They record the pronoun in 集韻 and quote second-person uses from historical texts, but the exact earliest surviving written attestation and the dates of the quoted wording are unresolved. A modern small-seal-style rendering is explicitly a font construction, not evidence for an ancient form.

The relationship of 尔 to 爾 belongs to the reported history of 尔 itself: it is described as a shortened form of 爾, which had uses meaning “you/your.” This does not establish that 尔 depicts an object or explain its proposed phonetic function in 你.

uncertainties.text: The dossier contains both a phono-semantic analysis (亻 for meaning, 尔 for sound) and an ideographic proposal (人 and 尔 contributing “person” and “you”). No inspected paleographic source directly analyzes 你’s formation, so neither construction is established by the supplied historical evidence.

No original depicted object or independently recoverable object-name pronunciation for 尔 is established. The evidence therefore does not support an account in which 你 was borrowed from an object-name.
The dictionaries list plural, possessive, and generic uses, but the dossier gives no dated sequence or supported semantic links among them.

senses.period: dating unresolved; cited in 集韻 and historical texts
senses.text: The dictionaries record 你 with the gloss 汝也 (“you”) and cite second-person uses. The evidence supports this use but does not establish the exact earliest surviving attestation or the date of the cited wording.
The character dictionaries report these uses, but their listings do not establish when they arose or how they relate to the singular pronoun.

limitations.text: The supplied evidence does not establish a chronology or semantic development connecting the reported plural, possessive, and generic uses with the singular second-person pronoun.

overview.text: 你 means “you,” usually addressing one person. Its visible left side 亻 represents a person; the right side 尔 is proposed as a sound cue, though that historical role is not firmly established.

components.text: 亻 contributes the person meaning in the proposed analysis; it is the side form of 人.
尔 is proposed as the sound element. The modern Mandarin readings ěr and nǐ can be compared, but do not prove the historical link.

relationships.text: In the proposed analysis of 你, 亻 represents a person and contributes the semantic category.

尔 is proposed as the sound element in one analysis of 你. The modern Mandarin pair is ěr and nǐ, but the inspected evidence does not establish a historical sound relation; a competing ideographic analysis is also reported.
